name: Hair transplant tourism (Turkey)

image.caption: MCAN Health - Hair Transplant in Turkey

lead: Hair transplant tourism in Turkey means flying abroad, usually to Istanbul, for a hair transplant sold as a bundle that can include the surgery, hotel, airport transfers and a translator. The appearance payoff is a fuller hairline and denser crown using the patient's own donor hair, at a price that people describe as much lower than in the US or UK.

The Turkish Health Tourism Association has estimated that about 1 million people travelled to Turkey for hair transplants in 2022, spending roughly $2 billion. Published peer-reviewed data on complication rates for this specific market are scarce; most of what is known comes from press reports, professional-society warnings and clinic-reported figures.

paras: Patients typically choose a clinic through social media or word of mouth, send photos for a remote assessment, and travel for a stay of a few days. The procedure itself is usually follicular unit extraction (FUE), in which grafts are taken one by one from the back and sides of the scalp and implanted in the thinning area. Many people pair it with medication or follow-up photos to track growth over the following year.

The International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery has warned about so-called black market clinics that use unlicensed practitioners or rush many patients through each day, with reported outcomes including infections, scarring and poorly designed hairlines. Press reports have described over-harvested donor areas and at least one death after surgery at an Istanbul clinic. The usual risks of any hair transplant, such as temporary shock loss and graft transection, also apply.

angle.text: A hair transplant moves permanent donor follicles from the back of the scalp to the hairline or crown, which can restore frontal framing and density. Travelling to Turkey is chosen by people mainly because the bundled price is lower than quotes at home, which makes a larger session affordable.

lead: Hair transplant tourism in Turkey is the practice of travelling to the country, most often to Istanbul, to have a hair transplant as part of a bundled package. People use it to rebuild a receding hairline or thinning crown, which changes how the face is framed and how young or full the head of hair looks. The surgery moves a person's own permanent follicles from the back and sides of the scalp to the thinning area, and packages commonly cover the operation, accommodation, transfers and translators, advertised heavily on social media and at airports.[1][2]

The scale is large and the figures come from industry and government sources that do not always agree. The Turkish Health Tourism Association has estimated that about 1 million people travelled to Turkey for hair transplants in 2022, spending around $2 billion, while Health Ministry data put total medical tourists at about 2 million in 2024.[1] A decade earlier, trade coverage cited official figures of roughly 100,000 hair-transplant visitors in 2015 out of 746,000 medical tourists.[3] Reported prices are far below Western quotes: one patient interviewed by public radio paid about $3,400 including flights and lodging, while a 2023 American Society of Plastic Surgeons study put typical US prices above $13,000.[1] Wikipedia's article on hair transplantation likewise cites an average of about US$1.07 per graft in Turkey against up to US$7 in Canada.[2]

Outcomes are described in very different ways. Patients on forums such as T Nation report good results, for example a co-worker who returned with a full head of hair and a friend whose surgery and holiday together cost about what the surgery alone would have cost at home.[4][5] Professional societies, notably the International Society of Hair Restoration Surgery (ISHRS), acknowledge that reputable physicians in many countries perform excellent transplants, while warning since 2014 and 2016 about unlicensed clinics where technicians do work that should be done by doctors.[6][6] Journalists describe a wide quality range among an estimated 5,000 clinics in Istanbul.[1]

Peer-reviewed research specific to this market is thin. Studies of complications after cosmetic surgery abroad exist, but they cover other procedures and destinations, and no published controlled study compares hair transplants done in Turkish medical-tourism clinics with those done at home.

paras: The procedure most associated with the trend is FUE, in which individual follicular units of one to four hairs are removed with small circular punches under local anaesthetic and implanted into the recipient area. Wikipedia notes it leaves small punctate scars rather than the linear scar of strip surgery, has a shorter recovery, and is slower and more skill-dependent, with some surgeons reporting a lower yield of surviving follicles; very large two-day sessions of roughly 2,500 to 3,000 grafts are described as possible.[2][7]

Packages in Turkey are typically all-inclusive, bundling the operation with hotels, transfers, translators and sightseeing.[1] Hair transplants are generally not covered by health insurance in most countries, which the ISHRS names as one reason lower prices abroad appeal.[6] Clinics advertise through TikTok and Instagram; public radio described clinic waiting rooms that play reels of satisfied clients, presenting surgery as a lifestyle upgrade.[1]

Clinic-reported figures are part of the picture. Smile Hair Clinic in Istanbul, which opened in 2018, told public radio it treats about 5,000 patients a year, roughly a third from the US, and advertises a 90 to 95 percent success rate, which is the clinic's own figure.[1] Its co-founder told Daily Sabah in 2023 that US patients had risen by 150 percent after the pandemic and put US prices at $7,000 to $15,000 against $4,000 to $10,000 in Turkey.[8] Earlier trade coverage quoted licensed clinics from about $1,500 and unlicensed operators from about $800 in 2016.[3]

Hair transplantation itself has a long history. Wikipedia traces scalp-hair grafting to 1897, small-graft work by Okuda in Japan in the 1930s, and the 1950s finding by Norman Orentreich that transplanted hair keeps the growth pattern of its donor site. FUE was described by Masumi Inaba in 1988 and published by Rassman, Bernstein and colleagues in 2002, and robotic devices received FDA clearance in 2009 (NeoGraft) and 2011 (ARTAS).[2][7] The extraction-based method suited high-volume clinics with trained teams, and it is the technique most associated with the Turkish market.

Turkey's health tourism sector grew through the 2010s. A regulation on international health tourism and tourist health took effect on 13 July 2017, and almost 178 thousand tourists visited for health purposes in the first half of 2018, most treated in private hospitals.[9] By 2015 trade coverage already counted over 100,000 hair-transplant visitors, with nearly two-thirds from the United Arab Emirates, and officials said more than 200 transplants were performed daily.[3] Travel agencies acted as intermediaries who received commissions from clinics per patient.[3]

The market then widened from the Gulf to Europe and North America. Industry figures cited by public radio suggest about 1 million visitors in 2022, and a clinic co-founder attributes growth in US patients partly to price gaps after the pandemic.[1][8] Public radio quotes a psychologist, Glen Jankowski, who argues that heavy advertising makes many people anxious about hair loss regardless of how much hair they have; clinics, in turn, present transplants as unremarkable.[1] Trade and press accounts credit celebrity and influencer discussion with helping make Istanbul's reputation, though no systematic study of that effect has been published.

Supporters say Turkish clinics perform the procedure at very high volume, so surgeons and technical teams become highly practised, and that the price difference reflects lower local costs rather than lower quality. Forum members describe friends who took a trip to Europe, had several thousand follicles transplanted via FUE, and came back with results nobody could detect.[5] Others say the transplant in Turkey cost the same as the operation alone at home, and a T Nation poster describes a co-worker whose receding hairline became a full head of hair.[4][5]

Combining procedures is a recurring theme in looksmaxxing forums, where Turkey is discussed as a destination for other cosmetic surgery. Members share quotes for nose and chin surgery including a week's stay, and one announced a trip to Antalya for a long list of facial procedures at once; others warn about named surgeons they have read negative reports about.[10][11][12] These are individual posts, not surveys.

Clinics emphasise physician credentials, follow-up periods and success rates; Smile Hair Clinic's co-founder says patients are followed for up to about a year and a half.[8] The ISHRS's position, by contrast, is that patients should ask who evaluates them and who performs each step, including incisions and graft harvesting.[6][6]

Under Turkish rules described by trade press, hair transplant surgery may be performed only in a registered hospital by a doctor, dermatologist or plastic surgeon, with an emergency unit and at least one operating room.[3][13] Coverage in 2016 reported that stricter hospital requirements had pushed some operators into private clinics, residential buildings and offices, and quoted a Turkish surgeon saying unlicensed sites used technicians, students and sometimes people with no medical training.[3][13] The same coverage cited a figure of six in ten Istanbul clinics operating illegally; the figure is a press estimate, not an official audit.[3][13]

The Turkish Society of Plastic Reconstructive and Aesthetic Surgeons and the ISHRS have both issued warnings about unlicensed clinics.[3] Public radio reported in 2025 that the Health Ministry had pledged stricter oversight and more inspections, while critics say the number of clinics, estimated around 5,000 in Istanbul, makes enforcement difficult; the Smile Hair co-founder himself described a Wild West atmosphere in which patients must research clinics.[1]

Cross-border recourse is a further issue raised by commentators. Travel insurance often excludes complications of elective surgery, and surgeons at home may be asked to repair work without full records; these points come largely from clinic and law-firm commentary rather than studies.[6]

The ISHRS's 2016 press release warned of a technician-run black market in Turkey and of Turkish technician groups operating under licensed doctors' names in Germany, the Netherlands and Belgium; it described risks including misdiagnosis of other hair disorders and unnecessary surgery. It noted that physician-reported surgical hair restoration procedures worldwide rose 76 percent between 2006 and 2014 to 397,048.[6] The society is a physician organisation that advocates physician-performed surgery.[6]

Peer-reviewed data on this specific market are limited. A retrospective review at Khoula Hospital in Oman of 191 patients treated after aesthetic surgery abroad between 2013 and 2023 found high rates of wound infection and admission, mostly after body contouring in Iran, India and Thailand; only three patients had hair transplants and complications for them were not reported separately.[14] A review of Turkish Court of Cassation decisions from 2013 to 2023 on minimally invasive cosmetic interventions found hair transplantation in one of 49 cases; most involved laser epilation in beauty salons, and 26.5 percent involved a person without required training.[15] A 2021 US survey of 484 adults found that lower prices, shorter waits and privacy were the most-cited advantages of cosmetic surgery abroad and complications, lack of follow-up and distance the main disadvantages.[16]

Public radio also reports that the procedure is generally considered safe when a skilled surgeon performs it, while Jankowski cautions that harvesting very large numbers of follicles in one session can affect blood pressure and that some patients are steered to minoxidil or finasteride without full informed consent.[1]

Reported problems include infection, scarring, poorly designed hairlines and over-harvested donor areas.[1][6] Press coverage has described a French student told by a Belgian specialist that about 1,000 of 4,000 harvested grafts would not regrow.[1] A Greek television programme, reported by To Vima, featured a patient who paid 1,700 euros against about 5,000 quoted at home, says he later learned a beautician performed the work, and needed corrective surgery; the article presents this as patient allegation.[17]

In late July 2025 a 38-year-old British man, Martyn Latchman, died after falling ill at Dr Cinik clinic in Istanbul. The clinic said he became unwell during preparation before the transplant began and that pre-operative tests had cleared him; local media said he fell ill during or after a five-hour procedure. Istanbul's health directorate opened an investigation, and no findings were reported in the coverage consulted.[18] The UK Foreign Office is reported to have counted at least six British nationals who died in Turkey in 2024 after medical treatment including cosmetic surgery.[18]
General hair transplant effects also apply: temporary shock loss, graft transection, pit scarring in the donor area, and poorer graft survival in smokers.[2][7]

No studies found. Published research on hair transplantation in general exists, and studies of complications after cosmetic surgery abroad cover other procedures, but no controlled trial has compared outcomes of surgery performed in Turkish medical-tourism clinics with surgery at home.

lore.intro: Hair transplants in Turkey come up repeatedly on forums as an affordable route to a restored hairline and as a base for combined cosmetic surgery trips, alongside warnings about clinic quality.[5][10][11]
